newsitem.title: USA: U.S. concerned about trend in exports to China.
newsitem.headline: U.S. concerned about trend in exports to China.

text.p: The United States is concerned that the growth in U.S. exports to China has slowed considerabily after increasing substantially earlier in the decade, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Tuesday.
"We are in the process of looking into the range of causes of that rather diminished export performance," Barshefsky told the House Ways and Means trade subcommittee.

The $38 billion U.S. trade deficit with China was a matter of concern, Barshefsky said. The concern was not the consumer goods that China exports to the U.S. market, but rather the lack of growth in U.S. sales to China.

Barshefsky told the panel that, after strong growth from 1992 to 1995, U.S. exports to China grew by only 1.9 percent last year. At the same time, European and Japanese exports to China grew by double digits, she added.
She said the slowdown in U.S. exports was due partly to lower farm sales because of China's bumper crop last year. She added that the United States needed to have better access to China's markets.

"As we move into 1997, we see a further dampening of our exports to China," Barshefsky said. She said Japan and Europe were experiencing a slowdown in export growth to China this year as well, as China brings in more goods from other Asian countries and Latin America.

The huge U.S. deficit with China has played a large part in the debate on whether the United States should maintain China's Most Favored Nation trade status. Opponents of China's MFN status told the panel that the deficit would likely rise to $50 billion this year.

The House Ways and Means Committee is scheduled to vote on a resolution, sponsored by Rep. Jerry Solomon, R-N.Y., that would disapprove President Clinton's decision to renew China's MFN status for another year.

A majority of Ways and Means members support China MFN and the committee is expected to decide to send the measure to the full House for a vote with a recommendation that fellow lawmakers reject it, Congressional aides said.
